title: San Francisco Administrative Code § 37.15 — Reporting Obligations; Licensing
verbatim_quote: Owners of residential dwelling units subject to this Chapter 37 shall be required to report certain information about their units to the Rent Board ... For condominium units and units in buildings with fewer than 10 units, the information shall be reported commencing March 1, 2023 and updated annually by March 1 of each successive year. ... If a landlord has substantially complied with the obligation to report information about a rental unit as required under this Section 37.15, the landlord shall receive a license to impose rent increases on tenants in that unit under Sections 37.3(a)(1)-(2). If the landlord has not substantially complied with the reporting obligation, then the license to impose rent increases shall be temporarily suspended during the period of the landlord's noncompliance ... a tenant shall not be obligated to pay the increased rent for months during the period of suspension.
used_for: Mandatory annual Housing Inventory reporting for 1–9 unit buildings (including individual 2-unit owners), Rent Increase License issuance, suspension during non-compliance, and prospective-only restoration.

title: The Rent Board Housing Inventory (Official Reporting & License Guidance)
verbatim_quote: All owners of residential property are required to report. If you own residential property, you are required to report into the Housing Inventory online through the Rent Board Portal. Property owners who have tenants will receive a rent increase license after the submission. ... Reporting is free and can be done online 24/7. ... Deadline: March 1 of every year. You can still make a Housing Inventory submission and receive a rent increase license after the deadline. However, your rent increase notice will not be enforceable without having a rent increase license on the effective date of the notice. ... The rent increase license does not need to be included with your rent increase notice.
used_for: Step-by-step Housing Inventory workflow, free 24/7 online submission, automatic license generation, March 1 annual deadline, effective-date enforceability gate, and public tenant lookup.

title: San Francisco Rent Board Housing Inventory & Fee Portal
verbatim_quote: Welcome to the San Francisco Rent Board's Housing Inventory and Fee Portal. The Portal is a secure database that allows users to view property information, comply with the City's Housing Inventory requirements, and pay annual Rent Board fees. Property Owners/Managers: Submit information about your units to comply with the City's Housing Inventory requirements; Obtain a License to increase rents for tenants covered by Rent Control ... Tenants: View status of landlord's current License to increase rent for a unit.
used_for: Official online portal URL for creating an owner account, reporting units, downloading Rent Increase Licenses, paying the annual Rent Board Fee, and tenant license verification.

title: Information for Lessors of Residential Real Estate
publisher: San Francisco Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector (sftreasurer.org)
verbatim_quote: A person receiving rental income in connection with the operation of ... one residential structure consisting of fewer than four units; or one residential condominium is not, by reason of that fact alone, required to obtain a business registration certificate. If the same person engages in other business activities or incurs payroll expense, a business registration certificate may be required. ... Earning income from a short-term residential rental, regardless of the amount, is considered a business, therefore, you are required to register as a business. ... If you are a lessor of residential real estate in San Francisco, you must file a return unless you lease fewer than 4 units in any individual building.
used_for: Distinguishing the Treasurer's Business Registration Certificate from the Rent Board's Rent Increase License; conditional sub-4-unit residential structure exemption and Gross Receipts Tax threshold.

title: Register a Business — Who Needs to Register in San Francisco
publisher: San Francisco Office of the Treasurer & Tax Collector (sftreasurer.org)
verbatim_quote: Unless otherwise required, you do not need to register if your only business is the receipt of rental income in connection with the operation of any of the following: 1. A cooperative housing corporation ... 2. One residential structure consisting of fewer than four units; or 3. One residential condominium.
used_for: Confirming the express sub-4-unit carve-out from San Francisco Business Registration when long-term residential rental of one <4-unit building is the owner's sole SF business activity.

title: The Rent Board Fee (2026–2027 Rates, Deadlines, and Exemptions)
verbatim_quote: Please note that requesting a Rent Board Fee exemption does not satisfy Rent Board Housing Inventory reporting requirements. ... For the 2026-2027 tax year, the fee is: $59.00 per dwelling unit ... Deadline: March 1 of each year for the Rent Board Fee. A 5% late penalty will be added to the amount of the fee every month following March 1 (for a maximum penalty of 15%). ... Once you have paid the Rent Board fee in full, you can recover 50 percent of the fee from the tenants in occupancy of each unit if the tenant has been living in the unit as of November 1 of the applicable tax year.
used_for: 2026–2027 per-unit Rent Board Fee ($59.00), March 1 payment deadline, late penalty schedule, and distinction from the free Housing Inventory license.

title: Recover Part of Your Rent Board Fee from the Tenant
verbatim_quote: A landlord who has paid the Rent Board fee in full may be able to collect 50% of the Rent Board fee (excluding any late penalties that have been added to the fee) from the tenant(s) residing in the unit. ... The landlord may only bill the tenant for the Rent Board fee if the tenant was residing in the unit on or before November 1 in the year before the fee became due. ... A tenant's failure to pay the Rent Board fee is not a just cause for eviction. The landlord must go to Small Claims Court in order to collect an unpaid fee.
used_for: Rules for optional $29.50 (50%) Rent Board Fee recovery via security-deposit interest offset or separate 30-day billing statement (never added into base rent).

title: Form 571 — Allowable Annual Increases (Effective March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027)
publisher: San Francisco Rent Board (SF.gov Official PDF)
used_for: Authoritative schedule of San Francisco annual allowable rent increase percentages from April 1, 1982 through February 28, 2027.

title: Learn About Rent Increases in San Francisco (Includes Nov. 9, 2026 Pending Legislation Notice)
verbatim_quote: The allowed rent increase percentage in San Francisco is 1.6%. The percentage is effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Notice: Proposed Changes to Rent Increase Limitations (Posted November 9, 2026): The San Francisco Board of Supervisors is considering legislation (File No. 261020) that would temporarily limit the combined amount of banked rent increases and capital improvement rent increases that may be imposed on rent-controlled units to 10% per year. If enacted as currently proposed, the legislation would apply to banked rent increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026 ... This legislation has not been enacted and is subject to change. ... Landlords must calculate the rent increase on the tenant's base rent only. ... Rent increases cannot be rounded up to the nearest dollar. ... A landlord cannot charge additional rent simply because a new (or additional) roommate has moved into a unit with the existing tenant.
used_for: 1.6% current rate, base-rent-only rule, prohibition on rounding up, 12-month anniversary rule, 30/90-day + 5-day mail notice summary, roommate surcharge prohibition, and the November 9, 2026 File #261020 retroactive-cutoff warning.

title: Banked Rent Increases (Includes Nov. 9, 2026 Pending Legislation Notice)
verbatim_quote: Posted November 9, 2026: ... If enacted as currently proposed, the legislation would apply to banked rent increases noticed on or after September 15, 2026 ... This legislation has not been enacted and is subject to change. ... A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase. If less than 24 months pass, the skipped increase is lost and cannot be imposed at a later date. ... Banked increases do not have to be approved by the Rent Board, but must be calculated correctly. They cannot be compounded or prorated. To calculate the total banked rent increase, add the percentage amounts for each year banked together. Then multiply the banked percentage amount by the tenant's current base rent.
used_for: Additive (non-compounded) banking calculation, partial-increase banking, 24-month no-increase agency explanation, no Board pre-approval requirement, and the Nov. 9, 2026 File #261020 warning.

title: San Francisco Administrative Code § 37.3 — Rent Limitations
verbatim_quote: (a)(1) Annual Rent Increase. On March 1 of each year, the Board shall publish the increase in the CPI for the preceding 12 months ... A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase. In no event, however, shall the allowable annual increase be greater than 7%. (2) Banking. A landlord who refrains from imposing an annual rent increase or any portion thereof may accumulate said increase and, subject to Section 37.15, impose that amount on the tenant's subsequent rent increase anniversary dates.
used_for: Statutory formula (60% of Bay Area CPI-U, 7% ceiling), statutory linkage to § 37.15 licensing, banking authority, and prohibition on additional-occupant surcharges.

title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations Part IV — §§ 4.10 (Notice) & 4.12 (Banking)
verbatim_quote: Section 4.10(a) Those landlords not seeking a rental increase which exceeds the limitations set forth in Section 37.3 of the Rent Ordinance shall inform the tenant in writing on or before the date the notice is given of ... (1) Which portion of the rent increase reflects the annual increase, and/or banked amount, if any ... (b) Any rent increase which does not conform with the provisions of this Section shall render the entire rent increase null and void, unless the amount requested equals no more than the allowable annual and banked rent increase(s) ... Section 4.12(a) ... This banked amount may only be given at the time of an annual increase. ... A full 12 months must have elapsed from the date that an annual rent increase, or a portion thereof, could have been imposed before this banking section becomes applicable. Banked increases shall not be compounded and shall not be rounded up ... (b) In order to impose an accumulated rent increase the landlord shall: (1) inform the tenant, on or before the date upon which the landlord gives the tenant legal notice, which portion of the rent increase reflects banked amount, and (2) the dates upon which said banked amount is based; provided, however, that failure to include such information shall not render the increase null and void.
used_for: Enacted regulation governing written breakdown of annual vs. banked portions, basis dates, 12-month banking accrual rule, non-compounding/no-rounding, and express non-void savings clauses in §§ 4.10(b) and 4.12(b).

title: Board of Supervisors File No. 261020 — Cap on Rent Increases for Rent-Controlled Units
jurisdiction: Local — Pending Proposed Legislation (NOT Enacted Law)
verbatim_quote: File #: 261020 Version: 1 | Name: Administrative Code - Cap On Rent Increases for Rent-Controlled Units | Type: Ordinance | Status: Pending Committee Action | Introduced: 9/15/2026 | In control: Land Use and Transportation Committee | Final action: [blank] | Enactment date: [blank] | Title: Ordinance amending the Administrative Code to provide that banked rent increases and capital improvement rent increases for rent-controlled units may not increase a tenant's rent by more than a total of 10% per year, for the next three years; and making various non-substantive changes.
used_for: Confirming on 2026-11-10 that File #261020 remains Pending Committee Action (introduced 9/15/2026, not enacted law) and verifying its proposed 3-year 10%/year cap on combined banked + capital-improvement increases.

title: Learn About San Francisco Rental Laws (June 13, 1979 Coverage & Exemptions)
verbatim_quote: Many residential units built on or before June 13, 1979 have both rent control and eviction protection. ... If your unit was built before June 14, 1979, and is not used as a single family dwelling, it may have both: Rent control; Eviction protection. ... Rent Board counselor 415-252-4600. Monday through Friday, 9 am to 12 pm and 1 to 4 pm.
used_for: Rent Ordinance coverage baseline for a multi-unit residential building constructed in 1940 (pre-June 13, 1979), exemption categories requiring parcel/CO verification, and Rent Board counseling phone line.

title: Rent Increases Under Section 6.14 and Costa-Hawkins
verbatim_quote: Rules and Regulations Section 6.14 provides for an unlimited rent increase on remaining occupants when the last original occupant vacates the unit, as long as the landlord timely served all remaining occupants with a written '6.14 notice.' ... Generally, sixty days is considered reasonable. ... Costa-Hawkins provides that when the last original occupant no longer permanently resides in the unit, the landlord may impose an unlimited rent increase on a lawful subtenant or assignee who did not reside in the unit prior to January 1, 1996. ... In addition, a co-tenant, as opposed to a subtenant, is not subject to such a rent increase, regardless of when the co-tenant moved in.
used_for: Unit 1 April 1, 2026 partial occupant change analysis: why no market reset is allowed while an original occupant remains, the 60-day § 6.14 notice rule, and the co-tenant vs. subtenant distinction.

title: Rent Board Rules and Regulations Part VI — §§ 6.13 (Additional Occupants) & 6.14 (Subsequent Occupants)
verbatim_quote: Section 6.13: No extra rent may be charged solely for an additional occupant to an existing tenancy (including a newborn child), regardless of the presence of a rental agreement or lease which specifically allows for a rent increase for additional tenants. Such provisions in written or oral rental agreements or leases are deemed to be contrary to public policy. Section 6.14(b): ... Failure to give such a notice within 60 days of the landlord's actual knowledge of the occupancy by the subsequent occupant(s) establishes a rebuttable presumption that notice was not given within a reasonable period of time.
used_for: Voidness of any lease surcharge for additional occupants (§ 6.13) and the 60-day rebuttable presumption for written § 6.14 notices to subsequent occupants.

title: Petition for a Determination Pursuant to Section 6.14 and/or Costa-Hawkins
verbatim_quote: A landlord is not required to file a petition with the Rent Board for approval of a rent increase pursuant to Section 6.14 or Costa-Hawkins Section 1954.53(d). However, if a landlord is unsure whether a rent increase is justified, the landlord may file a petition at the Rent Board to seek a determination that either or both sections authorize a rent increase. ... Section 6.14 requires the last original occupant to 'vacate' the unit, while Costa-Hawkins only requires the last original occupant to no longer 'permanently reside' in the unit.
used_for: Optional Rent Board determination petition (Form 537) and the legal distinction between 'vacate' (§ 6.14) and no longer 'permanently reside' (Costa-Hawkins).

title: California Civil Code § 1954.53 — Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (Vacancy & Partial Occupancy)
verbatim_quote: (d)(2) If the original occupant or occupants who took possession of the dwelling or unit pursuant to the rental agreement with the owner no longer permanently reside there, an owner may increase the rent by any amount allowed by this section to a lawful sublessee or assignee who did not reside at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996. (3) This subdivision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy of a dwelling or unit where one or more of the occupants of the premises, pursuant to the agreement with the owner provided for above, remains an occupant in lawful possession of the dwelling or unit.
used_for: State statutory bar on vacancy decontrol in Unit 1 because original occupant Tenant A remains in lawful possession after April 1, 2026, plus substandard-citation bar under § 1954.53(f).

title: California Civil Code § 1947.12 & SF Rent Board AB 1482 Guidance
verbatim_quote: (a)(1) ... an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower ... (d) This section shall not apply to the following residential real properties: ... (3) Housing subject to rent or price control through a public entity's valid exercise of its police power consistent with Chapter 2.7 (commencing with Section 1954.50) that restricts annual increases in the rental rate to an amount less than that provided in subdivision (a).
used_for: Confirming why California's AB 1482 cap (8.8% in SF for 8/1/2026–7/31/2027) does NOT apply to SF rent-controlled units governed by the stricter 1.6% annual cap.

title: The California Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482) — SF Rent Board Report
verbatim_quote: The maximum rent increase for units under AB 1482 from August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027 is 8.8% in San Francisco. This does NOT apply for units under the rent increase limitations of the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. ... If a unit is already covered by San Francisco's local eviction and/or rent increase regulations, the unit remains subject to those local regulations and the statewide law does not remove or replace those tenant protections.
used_for: Official confirmation of the 8.8% AB 1482 figure (8/1/2026–7/31/2027) and its express non-applicability to units covered by the SF Rent Ordinance.

title: California Civil Code § 827 — Written Notice & Service of Rent Increases (30 vs. 90 Days)
verbatim_quote: (b)(1) In all leases of a residential dwelling ... from week to week, month to month, or other period less than a month, the landlord may increase the rent provided in the lease or rental agreement, upon giving written notice to the tenant, as follows, by either of the following procedures: (A) By delivering a copy to the tenant personally. (B) By serving a copy by mail under the procedures prescribed in Section 1013 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (2) If the proposed rent increase for that tenant is 10 percent or less ... the notice shall be delivered at least 30 days before the effective date ... (3)(A) If the proposed rent increase for that tenant is greater than 10 percent ... the notice shall be delivered at least 90 days before the effective date of the increase.
used_for: Mandatory service methods (personal delivery or CCP § 1013 mail only — not email/text alone) and 30-day (<=10%) vs. 90-day (>10% cumulative in 12 months) advance notice thresholds.

title: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1013 — Service by Mail Extensions (+5 / +10 / +20 Days)
verbatim_quote: (a) ... Service is complete at the time of the deposit, but any period of notice ... shall be extended five calendar days, upon service by mail, if the place of address and the place of mailing is within the State of California, 10 calendar days if either the place of mailing or the place of address is outside the State of California but within the United States ... and 20 calendar days if either the place of mailing or the place of address is outside the United States ... (b) The copy of the notice or other paper served by mail pursuant to this chapter shall bear a notation of the date and place of mailing or be accompanied by an unsigned copy of the affidavit or certificate of mailing.
used_for: Statutory +5 calendar day extension for California-to-California mail (+10 out-of-state, +20 international) and mandatory date/place-of-mailing notation.

title: California Tenants — A Guide to Residential Tenants' and Landlords' Rights and Responsibilities (Rev. 2022)
publisher: California Department of Real Estate / Hosted by California Courts (courts.ca.gov)
verbatim_quote: Fixed-term tenancies are tenancies that last for a set amount of time and have a defined expiration date, such as six months or one year. ... There are some advantages to having a fixed-term tenancy. For instance, the landlord cannot raise the tenant's rent during the tenancy, unless the rental agreement expressly allows rent increases.
used_for: Fixed-term lease bar: verifying why Unit 1's April 1, 2026 tenancy agreement must be inspected before serving any increase prior to expiration of any fixed term.

title: California Civil Code §§ 1942.4 (Substandard Habitability Bar) & 1942.5 (Retaliation Protection)
verbatim_quote: § 1942.5(a): If the lessor retaliates against the lessee because of the exercise by the lessee of the lessee's rights under this chapter or because of the lessee's complaint to an appropriate agency as to tenantability of a dwelling, and if the lessee of a dwelling is not in default as to the payment of rent, the lessor may not ... increase the rent, or decrease any services within 180 days ... (f) This section does not limit in any way the exercise by the lessor of the lessor's rights under any lease or agreement or any law pertaining to the hiring of property or the lessor's right to do any of the acts described in subdivision (a) or (d) for any lawful cause.
used_for: 180-day retaliation screening window, good-faith lawful-cause rule, and pre-notice habitability verification.

title: California Civil Code § 1942.4 (Unabated Code Violation Bar on Rent Increases) & SF Failure to Repair Petitions
verbatim_quote: § 1942.4(a): A landlord of a dwelling may not demand rent, collect rent, issue a notice of a rent increase, or issue a three-day notice to pay rent or quit ... if all of the following conditions exist prior to the landlord's demand or notice: (1) The dwelling substantially lacks any of the affirmative standard characteristics listed in Section 1941.1 ... (2) A public officer or employee ... has notified the landlord or the landlord's agent in writing ... (3) The conditions have existed and have not been abated 35 days beyond the date of service of the notice.
used_for: Statutory prohibition and $100–$5,000 special damages + attorney's fees liability if a rent increase notice is issued with an unabated >35-day housing/DBI citation.

title: Failure to Repair and Maintain Petitions & Rent Board Referral Listing (94122 Legal Aid)
verbatim_quote: A tenant may petition for a deferral of the annual rent increase if the landlord has failed to perform requested repairs, replacement or maintenance as required by state and/or local law. ... If the petition is granted, the proposed rent increase will be deferred or postponed until the requested repairs are made. ... The petition must be filed no later than 60 days following the tenant's receipt of the rent increase notice.
used_for: 60-day tenant petition window (Form 516B) to defer an annual increase when requested legally required repairs remain incomplete.

title: Rent Board Referral Listing (Free & Low-Cost Tenant Legal Resources in SF / 94122)
verbatim_quote: Please note that you do not need a lawyer to file a petition at the Rent Board. ... Open Door Legal: Legal assistance to residents in service areas ... Sunset Office: 1722 Irving Street, San Francisco, CA 94122 ... Housing Rights Committee of SF: Free counseling ... San Francisco Tenants Union ... Bay Area Legal Aid.
used_for: Documenting official SF tenant counseling/legal referral organizations serving 94122 (including Open Door Legal's Sunset office on Irving St), while noting eligibility/scope limits.

title: Fair Housing & Anti-Harassment Laws: 42 U.S.C. § 3604, Cal. Gov. Code § 12955 (FEHA), Cal. Civ. Code § 51 (Unruh) & SF § 37.10B
publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office / California Legislative Information / SF.gov

To discriminate against any person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of sale or rental of a dwelling, or in the provision of services or facilities in connection therewith, because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin [and handicap under § 3604(f)(2)].

Code § 12955(a): It shall be unlawful: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
used_for: California protected classes (including source of income/housing vouchers, marital status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status) governing selective vs. uniform rent increases.

title: San Francisco Administrative Code § 37.10B — Tenant Harassment
verbatim_quote: (a) No landlord, and no agent, contractor, subcontractor or employee of the landlord shall do any of the following in bad faith: ... (5) Influence or attempt to influence a tenant to vacate a rental housing unit through fraud, intimidation or coercion ... (9) Violate any law which prohibits discrimination based on actual or perceived race, gender, sexual preference, sexual orientation, ethnic background, nationality, place of birth, immigration or citizenship status, religion, age, parenthood, marriage, pregnancy, disability, AIDS or occupancy by a minor child ... (c)(5) ... money damages of not less than three times actual damages ... or for statutory damages in the sum of one thousand dollars, whichever is greater ... and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
used_for: Local anti-harassment and anti-discrimination protections (adding age, immigration/citizenship status, occupancy by a minor child) and treble-damages + mandatory attorney's-fee remedies.

title: San Francisco Administrative Code § 37.10C — Use and Sale of Algorithmic Devices Prohibited
verbatim_quote: (b) Prohibition on Use. It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device described in subdivision (a) when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in San Francisco. Each separate month that a violation exists or continues, and each separate residential dwelling unit for which the landlord used the algorithmic device, shall constitute a separate and distinct violation. [Added by Ord. No. 224-24, effective October 14, 2024; amended by Ord. No. 169-25, effective October 6, 2025]
used_for: San Francisco's statutory ban on algorithmic revenue-management software using non-public competitor data ($1,000/month/unit civil penalty + attorney's fees), constraining corporate REITs and individual landlords alike.

title: U.S. Department of Justice Antitrust Division — Proposed RealPage Consent Judgment (Press Release 25-1111)
verbatim_quote: The Justice Department's Antitrust Division filed a proposed settlement today [November 24, 2025] to resolve the United States' claims against RealPage Inc. ... As alleged in Plaintiffs' complaint, RealPage's revenue management software has relied on nonpublic, competitively sensitive information shared by landlords to set rental prices. ... If approved by the court, the proposed consent judgment would require RealPage to: Cease having its software use competitors' nonpublic, competitively sensitive information to determine rental prices in runtime operation.
used_for: Documented federal antitrust enforcement context regarding institutional multifamily revenue-management software (accurately bounded as complaint allegations and a proposed Tunney Act consent judgment).

The RHFS collects data on: Property characteristics ... Rental status and monthly rents in residential buildings ... Property management and ownership status.
